title: The Best Leadership Reading List, August 2026
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: This monthly curated reading list gathers roughly a dozen leadership and management pieces under a Truman epigraph ('not all readers are leaders, but all leaders are readers'), and the curator adds a pull-quote of the argument for each rather than a bare link. The selections cluster around a few recurring themes: treating organizational change as an open-ended learning journey rather than a fixed plan, distinguishing failures (which happen despite good execution) from mistakes (which stem from poor judgment), and skepticism about AI's actual bottom-line payoff even as most employees report feeling more productive. Several items focus specifically on interpersonal leadership habits — admitting 'I don't know,' cultivating healthy conflict, and choosing friction over silence — while the closing book excerpt (The Fearless Organization) ties the whole list together around psychological safety as something leaders must deliberately build, not a personality trait some teams happen to have.
points: Frames organizational transformation as a 'learning journey' with an incompletely defined goal rather than a fixed plan to execute.
Draws a sharp line between failures (can happen despite good execution) and mistakes (stem from poor judgment or unawareness) — useful for how leaders assign accountability.
Notes a persistent gap between individual-level AI productivity gains (80% report improvement) and unmoved enterprise-level financial impact (37% EBIT contribution, flat year over year).
Collects several distinct arguments for the same underlying habit: leaders who visibly tolerate uncertainty, conflict, and being wrong build more trust than leaders who project constant confidence.
Closes on psychological safety as something leaders 'can and must help create' — a designed feature of the workplace, not an innate team trait.
quotes: A better approach is to manage transformation as a learning journey. By that, we mean a process with an incompletely defined goal that evolves as the organization makes decisions, learns from outcomes, and adjusts accordingly.
Distinguish failures from mistakes. Failures can happen despite good execution. Mistakes often stem from poor judgment, emotional reactions, or a lack of awareness about your circumstances.

Eight in ten respondents say AI has improved their own productivity. However, enterprise-level financial impact hasn't followed the same trajectory. The share of respondents reporting that AI has contributed to their organizations' EBIT is essentially unchanged from a year ago, at 37 percent.
The people who can never say "I was wrong" don't stop being wrong. They just stop finding out.
As a CEO, you need breadth over depth, delegation over mastery, judgment exercised through other people rather than applied directly to the work.
Organizations must find, and keep finding, new ways to create value to thrive over the long term. And creating value starts with putting the talent you have to its best and highest use.
Today's employees, at all levels, spend 50% more time collaborating than they did 20 years ago. Hiring talented individuals is not enough. They have to be able to work well together.
